summary: This informational RFC describes the Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015 block cipher known as Kuznyechik, which has a 128-bit block length and a 256-bit key length. It is one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: Kuznyechik is a block cipher described in the Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015. This RFC explains its parameters, transformations, key schedule, encryption, and decryption.

subtitle: An informational description of the Kuznyechik block cipher in GOST R 34.12-2015.

tldr.problem: GOST R 34.12-2015 defines the Kuznyechik block cipher, and implementers need a detailed description of its transformations and key schedule.
tldr.mechanism: Kuznyechik encrypts 128-bit blocks with a 256-bit key expanded into ten round keys. Its repeated transformations combine key XOR, byte substitution, and a linear transformation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7801 provides an informational description and test examples. It does not define modes of operation or state that the cipher is an Internet Standard.

sections.title: Scope and Background
sections.content:
RFC 7801 describes Kuznyechik, a block cipher with a 128-bit block length and a 256-bit key, from the Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015. The standard covers cryptographic techniques for information processing and protection, and its algorithms are designed for hardware and software implementation.

The RFC is an Independent Submission published for information. Its publication statement says that the RFC Editor makes no claim about the cipher's value for implementation or deployment and that the document is not a candidate for an Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is an information source about one cipher in a Russian cryptographic standard. It describes how the cipher works but does not recommend its use.

sections.title: The Cipher's Transformations
sections.content:
Kuznyechik operates on a 128-bit block, arranged as sixteen bytes. Its X transformation combines a block and a 128-bit value using exclusive-or. Its substitution S replaces each byte using a fixed nonlinear table, and S^(-1) applies the inverse table.

The R transformation shifts byte positions and calculates a new byte using a linear function over all sixteen bytes. The L transformation applies R repeatedly. The RFC defines these functions precisely so that implementations produce the same output.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher changes a block by combining it with a key, replacing bytes through a lookup table, and mixing byte positions. The RFC defines inverse operations so decryption can reverse the changes.

sections.title: Generating the Round Keys
sections.content:
The key schedule converts the 256-bit key into ten 128-bit round keys. The first two round keys are the left and right halves of the original key. The remaining keys are generated through repeated applications of the defined F transformation.

The transformation uses round constants derived from values 1 through 32. Four groups of eight steps generate the later round-key pairs. The encryption and decryption procedures use this same set of round keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher splits its 256-bit key into two initial round keys. It applies a repeated process to generate the other eight keys used during encryption.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
Encryption applies LSX with round keys K_1 through K_9, then applies a final key XOR with K_10. Each LSX step combines a key, substitutes bytes, and applies the linear transformation.

Decryption reverses the transformations and uses the round keys in reverse order. The RFC specifies the basic block cipher only; it does not define modes for processing messages longer than one block.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption repeats the same three transformations with successive keys, then applies one final key. Decryption reverses the transformations and uses the keys in reverse order.

sections.title: Informative Test Examples
sections.content:
The RFC includes examples of the substitution and linear transformations, a complete key schedule, and test encryption and decryption. It labels these examples informative, not a normative part of the standard.

In the test example, the plaintext 1122334455667700ffeeddccbbaa9988 is encrypted with the listed key to 7f679d90bebc24305a468d42b9d4edcd. The decryption example returns the original plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives sample inputs and outputs that can be compared with an implementation. These examples help illustrate the steps but are not part of the standard's normative definition.
